t.1.94.1: Thus that wise Śaṃtanu, honored by gods, kings and seers, righteous in spirit, was renowned in all the worlds as truthful in speech.
t.1.94.2: Self-restraint, generosity, forbearance, wisdom, modesty, steadfastness and supreme energy were ever present in Śaṃtanu, that bull among men of great spirit.
t.1.94.3: Thus that king, endowed with virtues and skilled in dharma and artha, was the protector of the Bharata lineage and of good people.
t.1.94.4: With a neck like a conch shell, broad-shouldered, and striding with the might of an elephant in rut, he was firmly resolved that dharma alone is higher than pleasure and wealth.
t.1.94.6: For the kings consecrated that protector of the earth, who abided by his own dharma and was the foremost of all knowers of dharma, in the sovereignty of a king of kings.
t.1.94.5: These qualities were present in the great-spirited Śaṃtanu, O bull of the Bharatas, and there was no kṣatriya equal to him in righteousness.
t.1.94.8: When the world was then protected by kings headed by Śaṃtanu, through the discipline of all the classes, the brahman held the foremost place.
t.1.94.7: Free from grief, fear and distress, sleeping and waking in happiness, the kings turned to the protector of the Bhāratas.
t.1.94.10: Dwelling in lovely Hāstinapura, the city of the Kurus, he ruled the earth bounded by the ocean.
t.1.94.9: The kṣatra served the brahma, and the viś were devoted to the kṣatra; and the Śūdras, attached to the brahma and the kṣatra, served the viś.
t.1.94.11: He was like the king of the gods, knowing dharma, truthful in speech and upright; through his practice of generosity, dharma and austerity he was endowed with the highest splendor.
t.1.94.12: Free from passion and hatred, he was as pleasing to behold as the moon; in splendor he resembled the sun, and in swiftness he equaled the rushing speed of the wind. In anger he was like Death, the Ender, and in forbearance he was equal to the earth.
t.1.94.13: While Śaṃtanu was protector of the earth, O king, there was no needless slaughter of cattle and boars, nor likewise of deer and birds.
t.1.94.15: Rites were then undertaken for the sake of sacrifices to the gods, the seers, and the ancestors, and no living creatures were slain unrighteously.
t.1.94.14: In a kingdom where dharma and brahman were held supreme, Śaṃtanu, disciplined and self-possessed, ruled all beings impartially, free from desire and passion.
t.1.94.16: That very king became the father of all beings, of the unhappy and the unprotected, and of those dwelling in animal wombs.
t.1.94.17: While he, the best of the lords of the Kurus, was the sovereign over kings of kings, speech rested upon truth, and the mind was devoted to generosity and dharma.
t.1.94.18: For sixteen years and eight, and four and eight more besides, finding no delight in women, he became a dweller of the forest.
t.1.94.21: Once, having pierced a deer with his arrow, King Śaṃtanu, following along the river Gaṅgā, saw the Bhāgīrathī with but little water.
t.1.94.19: Like him in form, like him in conduct, like him in behavior, and like him in learning, Gāṅgeya was born as his son, Devavrata by name, a Vasu.
t.1.94.20: He was expert in all weapons, and so too among the other kings; he was of great strength, great spirit and great valor, a mighty chariot-warrior.
t.1.94.22: Seeing her, Śaṃtanu, the bull among men, pondered: "Why is it that this best of rivers does not flow today as it did before?"
t.1.94.23: Then, searching for the cause, that great-minded one saw a boy endowed with beauty, tall and handsome to behold.
t.1.94.25: Seeing the river Gaṅgā covered with arrows near him, the king was amazed, having beheld a superhuman deed.
t.1.94.24: him, wielding a divine weapon like the god Puraṃdara, standing there after he had covered the entire Gaṅgā with sharp arrows.
t.1.94.26: Śaṃtanu had seen that son long ago, only at the moment of his birth; and so the wise king could not then summon the memory needed to recognize him as his own child.
t.1.94.27: But he, on seeing his father, bewildered him with his magic power; and having bewildered him, he then swiftly vanished right there.
t.1.94.28: Then, having seen that marvel there, King Śaṃtanu, suspecting it was his son, said to Gaṅgā, "Show him to me."
t.1.94.29: Gaṅgā, bearing a most excellent form, showed him that adorned boy, holding him by the right hand.
t.1.94.30: Adorned with ornaments and wearing a spotless garment, she stood before him, and though he had seen her before, Śaṃtanu did not recognize her.
t.1.94.32: The mighty one learned the Vedas together with their auxiliary branches from Vasiṣṭha himself; skilled in weapons, a supreme archer, he was equal to the king of the gods in battle.
t.1.94.33: He is ever esteemed by the gods and by the asuras, O Bhārata; whatever science Uśanas knows, this one knows it in its entirety.
t.1.94.31: The eighth son whom you, O king, formerly begot in me, this is he, your own, O tiger among men; take him to your home.
t.1.94.34: Likewise, whatever science the son of Aṅgiras, who is revered by gods and asuras, knows, that too, entire with its limbs and subsidiary limbs, is established in this great-armed, great-souled son of yours.
t.1.94.36: O king, this great archer, skilled in the duties and aims of kingship, your own son, a hero, given back by me, take him home, O hero.
t.1.94.35: Whatever weapon the mighty seer Rāma Jāmadagnya, unassailable by his foes, knows, that too is firmly established in him.
t.1.94.37: Thus permitted by her, Śaṃtanu took his son, who shone like the sun, and went back to his own city.
t.1.94.39: The greatly renowned son of Śaṃtanu, O bull among the Bharatas, delighted the Pauravas, his father, and the kingdom by his conduct.
t.1.94.38: The Paurava, having gone to his own city, which resembled the city of Puraṃdara, considered himself in his own mind a man whose every desire and aim had been fulfilled. Then, among the Pauravas, he consecrated his son as heir apparent.
t.1.94.40: Thus that lord of the earth, of immeasurable prowess, delighting together with his son, passed four years.
t.1.94.42: Seeking its source, he wandered all around; then he saw a maiden of the fishermen, divine in form.
t.1.94.41: Once, having gone to a forest near the river Yamunā, that lord of the earth caught the scent of an indescribable and most excellent fragrance.
t.1.94.43: As soon as he saw that dark-eyed maiden, he asked her: "Whose are you, and who are you, and what, timid one, do you wish to do?"
t.1.94.44: She said, "I am a fisherman's daughter; for the sake of dharma I ply this boat at the command of my father, the great-souled king of the fishermen. Blessings upon you!"
t.1.94.45: Seeing her, the fisherman's daughter, endowed with beauty, sweetness and fragrance and divine in form, King Śaṃtanu desired her.
t.1.94.47: And the king of the fishermen replied to that lord of the earth: "From the very moment of her birth, this fair-complexioned maiden was destined to be given to a worthy suitor. But there is a certain wish in my heart; learn what it is, O lord of men."
t.1.94.46: Going to her father, he then asked for her hand, and he questioned her father on his own behalf.
t.1.94.48: If you seek this girl from me as your lawful wife, O sinless one, then, since you are truthful in speech, make a compact with me on your truth.
t.1.94.50: Śaṃtanu said: Having heard your boon, O fisherman, I shall decide whether or not to grant it. If it is fit to be given, I will give it, but what ought not to be given I will by no means give.
t.1.94.49: On one condition I would give you this maiden, O king, for never will there be any suitor for me equal to you.
t.1.94.51: The son who may be born of her, he, O king, must be consecrated after you as king and lord of the earth, and no one else.
t.1.94.52: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Śaṃtanu did not wish to grant that boon to the fisherman, O Bhārata, even though he was burning with intense love born of the body.
t.1.94.53: Then that lord of the earth, still thinking only of the fisherman's daughter, returned to Hāstinapura, his mind stricken with grief.
t.1.94.54: Then one day his son Devavrata approached his father Śaṃtanu, who was grieving and lost in brooding thought, and spoke these words.
t.1.94.55: On every side there is safety for you, and all the kings are obedient to you; why then do you grieve here so constantly, distressed? And why, O king, as though lost in brooding, do you say nothing at all?
t.1.94.57: You alone are our offspring in this great lineage, O Bhārata, and mortals are impermanent; therefore I grieve, my dear son.
t.1.94.56: Thus addressed by his son, Śaṃtanu replied: "Without doubt, just as you describe me as given over to brooding, so indeed I am."
t.1.94.58: O Gāṅgeya, should misfortune somehow befall you, our lineage would cease to exist. Without doubt, you alone, a single son, are better than even a hundred sons.
t.1.94.60: The agnihotra, the three Vedas, and sacrifices together with their sacrificial fees: all these are not worth a sixteenth part of a son.
t.1.94.59: Nor do I wish to take wives again here needlessly; it is for the preservation of the lineage that I desire it, may good fortune be yours. Those who speak of dharma say that having only one son is the same as childlessness.
t.1.94.62: You are a hero, ever impatient of wrongs, and always devoted to arms, O Bhārata; therefore, O sinless one, your death will come from nothing other than a weapon.
t.1.94.61: So it is among men, and so it would be among all creatures as well: of what offspring is worth, O greatly wise one, I have no doubt. This is the eternal threefold Veda of the ancient and supreme ones.
t.1.94.64: Then, having learned that reason entirely and thus in full, the greatly wise Devavrata set out, reflecting upon it.
t.1.94.63: Thus I have fallen into doubt: if you were to perish, how would things be? So, dear son, the cause of my sorrow has been told to you in full.
t.1.94.65: Then at once he quickly went to the aged minister, devoted to his father's welfare, and, approaching him, asked him the cause of that grief of his father.
t.1.94.67: Then Devavrata, accompanied by elder kṣatriyas, approached the king of the fishermen and himself asked for the maiden on behalf of his father.
t.1.94.66: To that foremost of the Kurus, who questioned him in due form, he declared the boon he sought in return for that maiden, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.1.94.68: The fisherman received him in due form and, having honoured him, spoke to him as he sat in the royal assembly, O Bhārata.
t.1.94.69: You alone, O bull among men, are protector enough for Śaṃtanu, his son, the best among those who have sons; what words, then, shall I speak to you?
t.1.94.70: For who, passing up such a praiseworthy and desirable marriage alliance as this, would not regret it, even if he were Śatakratu himself?
t.1.94.71: And this is the offspring of a noble man who is your equal in virtues, from whose seed the illustrious Satyavatī was born.
t.1.94.72: Therefore, dear son, your father has often been extolled to me as the one worthy among all kings to marry Satyavatī, O Bhārata.
t.1.94.73: For even the divine seer Asita was once refused by me; that best of seers was an ardent suitor for Satyavatī.
t.1.94.75: For whoever has you as his foe, be he a gandharva or an asura, he could never live in happiness once you are angered, O scorcher of foes.
t.1.94.74: Yet, because I am the maiden's father, I shall say something, O bull of the Bharatas: in this matter I see only one fault, and a grave one, the rivalry it would bring.
t.1.94.76: This alone is the drawback here, O king, and there is no other at all; know this, O scorcher of foes, regarding the giving and the taking, and may good fortune be yours.
t.1.94.77: Thus addressed, O Bhārata, Gāṅgeya replied with fitting words for the sake of his father, while the kings listened.
t.1.94.79: I shall do this just as you say: the son who will be born of her shall be our king.
t.1.94.78: Accept this true resolve of mine, O best of the truthful: no one born, nor yet unborn, would dare to speak such words.
t.1.94.80: Thus addressed, the fisherman, intent on accomplishing a difficult deed for the sake of the kingdom, then replied to him once again, O bull of the Bharatas.
t.1.94.81: You alone, O righteous-souled one, are a sufficient protector for Śaṃtanu of boundless splendor and for the maiden as well; you are the master and the lord with authority over her giving in marriage.
t.1.94.83: O you who are devoted to truth and dharma, what you have vowed in the midst of the kings for the sake of Satyavatī is worthy of you alone.
t.1.94.82: But hear from me, gentle one, this word and also what must be done; I shall speak, O tamer of foes, in keeping with the custom of those who give away maidens.
t.1.94.84: It is not otherwise, mighty-armed one; there is no doubt at all about this. But concerning the offspring that may be born to you, about that we have a great doubt.
t.1.94.85: Having understood his intention, he who was wholly devoted to truth and dharma then gave his promise, O king, out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his father.
t.1.94.86: Devavrata said: O king of the fishermen, best of kings, hear these words of mine which I speak for my father's sake while these lords of the earth listen.
t.1.94.87: The kingdom, O lord of men, I have already renounced before; and now, for the sake of offspring too, I make this firm resolve.
t.1.94.88: From this day forth, O fisherman, I shall observe celibacy. Even though I am without a son, I shall have imperishable worlds in heaven.
t.1.94.89: Hearing those words of his, the righteous fisherman, his hair bristling with delight, replied to him, "I shall give her."
t.1.94.90: Then in the sky the Apsarases and the gods, together with the hosts of seers, rained down flowers and said, "This is Bhīṣma."
t.1.94.91: Then, for the sake of his father, he said to that glorious woman, "Mount the chariot, mother; let us two go to our own home."
t.1.94.92: Having spoken thus, Bhīṣma placed that beautiful woman on his chariot, and, having come to Hāstinapura, he made it all known to Śaṃtanu.
t.1.94.93: The kings, both assembled together and each one separately, praised that difficult deed of his, and they said, "This one is Bhīṣma, the Terrible."
t.1.94.94: Seeing that difficult deed done by Bhīṣma, Śaṃtanu, his father, pleased, himself granted him the boon of dying at his own will.
